title: The Easter homily
hook: his short Easter sermon, still read at Orthodox Easter: come, the first and the last

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Chrysostom, the golden mouth: honor him in the poor before you gild his altar. Did the gift come before the nicer thing? Day seven hundred forty-five.

Past midnight, deep into the Easter night service. Candles everywhere, people standing shoulder to shoulder, some of them worn out from the long fast, some of them who didn't fast at all and just walked in off the street. Then the priest reads a short sermon. Orthodox churches, and Eastern Catholic churches of the same Byzantine tradition, read it on Easter night. Tradition gives it to John Chrysostom. And it speaks straight to the person at the back who feels they don't belong here tonight.
screen: `EASTER NIGHT, PAST MIDNIGHT.` → `THE FASTERS AND THE LATECOMERS.` → `ONE SHORT SERMON.`

segments.voice: First, the welcome. The sermon opens by calling in everyone who loves God to enjoy this bright feast. Then it starts counting the hours, and you realize where you are. It's the parable of the workers in the vineyard, from Matthew. Some started at dawn. Some at the third hour, the sixth, the ninth. Some came at the eleventh hour, with barely any day left. Second, the surprise. In Jesus's parable, the landowner pays everyone the same, and the early workers grumble. The homily takes that story and turns it into an invitation. If you came at the eleventh hour, it says, don't be afraid because you're late. The Master is generous. He receives the last just as the first. He welcomes the deed, and honors even the intention. Third, the table. You who fasted and you who did not, the homily says, rejoice today. The table is full. Let no one go away hungry. Nobody is checking who earned a seat. Fourth, why. Because of what Easter is. The homily ends by turning to death itself, using Paul's words. In the Douay-Rheims: "O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?" Christ is risen, it says, and life reigns. So in the homily the generosity isn't a mood. It comes from the empty tomb: if death has lost, there's no reason to turn latecomers away. The eleventh hour, too, gets the full wage.
screen: `COUNTING THE HOURS.` · `THE LAST, JUST AS THE FIRST.` · `THE TABLE IS FULL.` · `DEATH, WHERE IS THY STING?` · then, large: `THE ELEVENTH HOUR TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invite someone who came late. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's arrived late to something you're part of. The new person on the team. The cousin who missed years of family dinners. The neighbor who just moved in. Someone who came back to church after a long time away. Hold their face for a moment. Then think of one small way to say, the table is full, there's room for you. An invitation to lunch. Saving them a seat. Introducing them to someone. If you pray, you can thank God for the ones who welcomed you when you were late. The bell holds the time.
Pascha. The Church's Greek name for Easter, and the night the homily tradition gives to Chrysostom welcomes even the eleventh hour's workers. Today's word.
Your line: the eleventh hour too. Today, make the invitation you just thought of, to the person who came late. Day seven hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: In Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic churches the Paschal homily attributed to John Chrysostom is read aloud at the Easter night service, and some Latin-rite Catholics read it during the Easter season.

original.note: Greek: Pascha, the church's name for Easter.

trapdoor: what you thought: the eleventh hour means a last-minute panic.
what it means: in Jesus's parable and in this homily, the latecomers who still get the full wage.
what a scholar hears: the Paschal homily retells Matthew 20:1–16 and ends with 1 Corinthians 15:55; its attribution to Chrysostom is traditional.

sources.ref: Paschal (Catechetical) Homily, attributed to John Chrysostom

notes: The homily is paraphrased throughout (the welcome, the hours, 'receives the last even as the first', 'welcomes the deed and honors the intention', 'you who fasted and you who did not', 'the table is full', 'let no one go away hungry', 'Christ is risen and life is set free'). Confirm.

Douay-Rheims 1 Corinthians 15:55 ('O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?'): confirm exact wording and order. The homily itself quotes it in the form 'O death, where is thy sting? O hell, where is thy victory?'.
Hook and howItsDone: read at the Paschal service in Orthodox churches and Byzantine-rite Eastern Catholic churches; 'some Latin-rite Catholics read it during the Easter season' is soft. Confirm.
Original: Greek Pascha; an etymology note (from Hebrew pesach) was left out under the claims rule.
Authorship: the script says only 'tradition gives it to John Chrysostom'.
Editor pass: cut 'every year' from the hook under the claims rule; 'life is set free' corrected toward the homily's 'life reigns'; the closing logic now reported as the homily's, not the narrator's.
Second editor pass: cut the count-like 'weeks of fasting' from the hook.

Audit pass (2026-10-01): hook called the setting 'the Easter vigil' (a Latin-rite term); in Orthodox and Byzantine churches the homily is read at the end of Paschal Matins, after midnight. Reworded to 'the Easter night service, past midnight' and the hook screen to match. Also: the voice says 'the priest reads'; in some parishes the deacon or bishop reads it. Keeper: confirm.
